::: {.lp-lede}
Instructing Machines is a fourteen-week introduction to programming for
molecular biology, written for students who will have a model at their side
from the first line they type. Every week pairs a piece of Python with a way
of working alongside an AI — and a way of checking what it hands back.
:::

:::

widgets &middot; MIT licensed]{.lp-counts}

:::

### Instructing machines: Brain <i class="bi bi-arrow-right-short"></i> AI <i class="bi bi-arrow-right-short"></i> Code <i class="bi bi-arrow-right-short"></i> Compute {.unnumbered} 

<!-- ::: {.lp-thesis}
Which is the argument of the whole course: an AI is useful to you up to the
limit of what you can specify and verify. Fourteen weeks of raising that limit.
::: -->


::: {.lp-panels}

::: {.lp-panel}
[<i class="bi bi-person"></i> Brain]{.lp-panel-label}

Your training is what lets you ask a real question about molecular biology,
find the answer yourself, and judge the answers you are handed.
:::

::: {.lp-panel}
[<i class="bi bi-code-slash"></i> Code]{.lp-panel-label}

Machine code is what tells a computer what to do. Python lets you write it in
something close to the plain English your brain already thinks in.
:::

::: {.lp-panel}
[<i class="bi bi-stars"></i> AI]{.lp-panel-label}

A model is good at turning a problem posed in human language into code that
runs. Knowing programming is what lets you steer it, and read what comes back.
:::

::: {.lp-panel}
[<i class="bi bi-cpu"></i> CPU]{.lp-panel-label}

Your brain is roughly two hundred times faster than a good laptop. But a CPU
will spend all of itself on one problem, if you can say what the problem is.
:::

:::

::: {.lp-thesis}
An AI is useful to you up to the limit of what you can specify and verify. The course spends fourteen weeks raising that limit.
:::


## Every week, two threads {.unnumbered}

A Python topic and an AI practice, taught together, applied to a project from
molecular biology.

::: {.lp-arc}

| Wk | Python | Working with an AI | Project |
|:---|:-------|:-------------------|:--------|
| 01 | Values, operators, logic | Meet the assistant | — |
| 02 | If-else, functions | The AI predicts, the widget proves | — |
| 03 | Objects, lists, dictionaries, tuples | How a model produces code, and why it can be wrong | Turtle |
| 04 | Iteration, testing | Ask it to explain, then confirm by running | Turtle |
| 05 | Data structures, files | Practical AI use | Turtle |
| 06 | Composition | Ask for another way | Translating ORFs |
| 07 | Classes, debugging | Let it draft a piece you can read and test | Primer analysis |
| 08 | Reading unfamiliar code | Tests are the contract | Pairwise alignment |
| 09 | Modules and packages | The AI invents functions; the docs are the test | Codon usage |
| 10 | Recursion, decomposition | Plan before you prompt | HIV sub-groups |
| 11 | Putting the pieces together | Delegate the full problem | Sequence trees |
| 12 | Dataframes | Learning with an AI; how you know a fact is true | Finding genes |
| 13 | Your own tool, start to finish | Finale: formulating, building, finishing | Genome assembly |
| 14 | Where you stand | Surviving AI &middot; the AI-off test | — |

:::

## What the material looks like {.unnumbered}

The notes are executable notebooks. Exercises come with widgets that step
through code line by line, so a claim about what the machine does can be
settled on the spot.

<!-- Replace with a real screenshot: notebook + step-through widget. -->
::: {.lp-shot}
[screenshot: notebook with the step-through widget]{.lp-shot-label}
:::

[A live demo of the same material runs in the browser through
[JupyterLite](demo/lab/index.html) — no install.]{.lp-caption}

```python
def gc_content(seq):
    """Fraction of G and C in a DNA sequence."""
    gc = seq.count("G") + seq.count("C")
    return gc / len(seq)

# The test is the contract. Ask the AI for the body, keep this.
assert gc_content("GCGC") == 1.0
assert gc_content("ATAT") == 0.0
```

[<i class="bi bi-mortarboard-fill"></i> For students]{.lp-audience-label}

### Fifteen minutes to your first line {.unnumbered}

The course folder, Python, the editor and the terminal are all set up in one
pass, most of which is waiting. You only do it once — see
@sec-getting_started.

By the end you can:

- Read code the way the machine does.
- Write Python to solve small problems.
- Break a problem into sub-problems and write them as testable functions.
- Verify code written by an AI, or by someone else.
- Judge how much of a task to hand over, and how much to keep.
- Explain why an AI is only as useful to you as your ability to check it.

[Getting started <i class="bi bi-arrow-right"></i>](python/getting_started.qmd){.lp-btn}

:::

### Take it and make it yours {.unnumbered}

Built for undergraduates in Molecular Biology and Molecular Medicine at
[Aarhus University](https://kursuskatalog.au.dk/en/course/133215/Bioinformatics),
and [MIT licensed](https://opensource.org/license/mit). If you teach a similar
course, fork it.

::: {.lp-list}
- Notes, slides, exercises and projects, all in the repository
- Seven notebook widgets, installable as packages
- A JupyterLite demo, so students can try before installing
- A written account of the course design and the AI arc
:::
